body:
A large language model (LLM) is an artificial intelligence system trained on a vast dataset to analyze, predict, and generate natural language. Popular LLMs include OpenAI’s GPT models, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini, which are often used for things like writing, editing, and coding.

Initially, LLM datasets mainly included text from sources like books, blogs, and even online forums. Modern LLMs now use multimodal data to expand use cases, such as powering conversational voice agents or making music.

Before implementing this technology, organizations often need answers to questions like: what is an LLM, how does an LLM work, and what architectures should the team use? This guide tackles these questions while also showing real-world applications of the technology and their tangible benefits.

## Summary

• A large language model (LLM) is an artificial intelligence model trained on vast datasets of text and multimodal datasets with the goal of analyzing, predicting, and generating output.

• The main difference between GPTs and LLMs is that GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is a specific family of LLMs created by OpenAI, whereas LLM is the umbrella term for models like Claude and Gemini.

• Generative AI is the broad category for models that create a wide range of content based on training data, while LLMs are a specialized subset of generative AI that focus on natural language processing.

• LLMs work by using transformer neural networks to break text into smaller units called tokens, and then predict the next token based on contextual information from the prompt and existing chat history.

• Practical large language model examples include customer service chatbots, automated writing tools, code generators, and natural language processing layers for voice applications.

## What is an LLM? The large language model definition

A large language model is an AI program built on deep learning neural networks for analyzing, predicting, and generating natural language. Developers trained these models on datasets that contain billions of works across books, academic papers, websites, and blogs. The term “large” refers to both the massive volume of data used to train these models and the billions of internal parameters that govern their behavior.

Large language models are a major shift from how earlier software worked; traditional software relied on explicit syntax commands but LLMs do not. Rather than processing each word in isolation, LLMs use contextual relationships to recognize complex linguistic patterns and grammar. They interpret unstructured human language and continue to respond to open-ended user prompts, adapting to context changes mid-conversation.

These advancements in natural language processing power ElevenAgents so that they understand complex customer intents and execute automated workflows.

## How do large language models work?

Large language models process text through artificial neural networks to analyze natural language input and generate relevant content. The process begins with tokenization, where the model splits input text into smaller units called tokens. The model then translates these tokens into numerical representations (called embeddings) to evaluate mathematical or statistical relationships across tokens.

Most modern LLM systems rely on the transformer neural network architecture. Transformers use self-attention mechanisms, which handle the work of evaluating the contextual relationships between tokens. The model predicts the most statistically probable token to complete a sequence by using learned patterns to calculate probability distributions.

Self-attention makes it possible for natural language processing models to maintain long-range context and adapt to shifts in the middle of a conversation. Platform integrations with ElevenAgents build on these capabilities to deliver low-latency, relevant responses that mirror natural human conversation.

## What is temperature in an LLM?

LLM temperature is a variable setting that developers can configure to determine how random an LLM’s outputs will be. LLMs generate the next token in a string of words by selecting the option that is most common. However, for every choice the LLM makes, there could be several other alternatives that have similar weighting.

By adjusting the LLM temperature, you change how strongly an LLM favors the most probable option. A low temperature setting would produce a standard and consistent output (as it would lean toward always choosing the most predictable next token in a string). On the other hand, a high temperature would deviate from the expected choice more frequently, producing more creative and varied outputs.

You should adapt your LLM temperature value to the task you want to achieve. Anything that needs an element of creativity should lean toward higher temperatures, while routine tasks or structured outputs (like data summaries) should lean lower.

## How are LLMs trained and fine-tuned?

Training LLMs requires a multistage process to transform raw text and multimodal data into functional language systems. Companies need advanced supercomputing capacity running for several months, whereas fine-tuning is a lighter process that customizes the existing base model.

Frontier AI companies tend to treat their exact training process as proprietary information and most do not disclose source code or weights. Nevertheless, training generally follows this process:

• Data collection and preprocessing: Developers build datasets from multiple sources with pre-training corpora that include trillions of tokens taken from terabytes of cleaned text. Scraping or mining text from internet sources is one of the main ways that companies build these datasets.

• Unsupervised pretraining: The large language model reads trillions of tokens to learn grammar rules, factual relationships, and linguistic context. It essentially pretrains itself through autoregressive language modeling
